options: Demographic variables measure only usage rate, so they cannot explain which product a person chooses
Demographic data cannot legally be used in Canada to market vehicles to individual consumers
Demographics describe who people are statistically, not the personalities, values or lifestyles that psychographics capture
Demographic variables always predict purchases perfectly, so the survey data must be inaccurate
questions.explanation: Demographics capture census-type facts; differences in values and personality (thrill-seeking versus practicality) are psychographic. Usage rate is a behaviouristic variable, not a demographic one.

questions.stem: Nike recently debuted Air Jordan XVII with a price tag of $200. The shoes arrived at shoe stores in a metallic silver briefcase instead of a shoebox. Nike is targeting a market it identifies as 'keepers,' people who buy the shoes, keep them under their bed and when friends come over, show them the shoes. Selling to the market segment called 'keepers' probably means that Nike is using which of the following types of customer characteristic variables to segment this market?
questions.explanation: 'Keepers' are defined by personality and lifestyle (collecting and showing off), which are psychographic variables. 'Usage' and 'behaviour' are tempting because the stem describes what people do, but keeping shoes unworn reflects personality, not how much or how they use the product.

questions.stem: Lifestyle, measured through consumers' activities, interests and opinions (AIO), together with personality and values, makes up which family of segmentation variables?
questions.explanation: Lifestyle (AIO), personality and values are psychographic variables. Behaviouristic variables cover product-related behaviour such as usage rate and benefits sought.

questions.stem: A fitness club is building four segments. Which one is based on a PSYCHOGRAPHIC variable rather than a behaviouristic one?
options: Members who visit the club five or more times a week
Former members who did not renew their membership last year
People who describe themselves as competitive achievers who love a challenge
People who sign up during the club's January New Year promotion
questions.explanation: Seeing oneself as a competitive achiever is personality/lifestyle, which is psychographic. Visit frequency is usage rate, former members is user status, and January sign-ups is purchase occasion; all three are behaviouristic.

questions.stem: Which of the following would NOT be classified as a psychographic variable?
questions.explanation: Usage rate (heavy, medium, light and non-users) is behaviouristic. Personality, values and attitudes all describe the consumer's inner life, which is psychographic.

questions.stem: Arctic Trail Outfitters wants to build its next campaign around psychographic segments. Which information should its research team collect?
options: Customers' ages, incomes and education levels
How often customers buy and which benefits they seek
Customers' provinces, city sizes and climates
Customers' activities, interests, opinions and values
questions.explanation: Psychographic segmentation uses lifestyle (activities, interests, opinions), personality and values. Ages and incomes are demographic, purchase frequency and benefits sought are behaviouristic, and provinces and climates are geographic.

questions.stem: Brightsmile toothpaste offers one version for people who want whiter teeth, one for people who want cavity protection, and one for people with sensitive teeth who want pain relief. Brightsmile is segmenting on:
questions.explanation: Grouping buyers by what they want the product to do for them is segmentation by benefits sought, a behaviouristic variable. Usage rate would group them by how much toothpaste they use.

questions.stem: A telecom company creates different offers for three groups: people who have never had its service, first-time subscribers, and customers who cancelled last year. Which behaviouristic variable is it using?
questions.explanation: Non-users, first-time users and ex-users are categories of user status. Loyalty status measures how committed current buyers are to the brand, and usage rate measures how much they use it.

questions.stem: The course describes behaviouristic variables as answering which question about a target market?
options: Where does it live and work?
What is its basic census-type information?
What attitudes, values and interests does it share?
How does it use and interact with the product?
questions.explanation: Behaviouristic = how the target market uses and interacts with the product (benefits sought, usage rate, user status, loyalty, occasion). The other questions describe geographic, demographic and psychographic variables.

questions.stem: A coffee chain notices that some customers always buy its brand and nothing else, while others buy whichever brand is on sale. Segmenting customers on this difference uses which variable?
questions.explanation: How committed a buyer is to one brand is loyalty status, a behaviouristic variable. It can sound like an attitude, but it describes the customer's buying relationship with the product, not their general personality or values.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a behaviouristic segmentation variable?
questions.explanation: Personality is psychographic. Benefits sought, purchase occasion, loyalty status, user status and usage rate are behaviouristic because they describe how people use and interact with the product.

questions.stem: The concept suggesting that 80 percent of a firm's sales are obtained from 20 percent of its customers is the:
questions.explanation: That is the 80/20 rule. Usage rate is the related variable (quantity consumed or store visits during a period) used to find the heavy users who produce most of the sales.

questions.stem: Lakeshore Pizza has 2,000 customers and annual sales of $500,000. If its sales follow the 80/20 rule exactly, about how much revenue comes from its 400 heaviest customers?
questions.explanation: 400 / 2,000 = 20% of customers. Under the 80/20 rule, they produce 80% of sales: 0.80 x $500,000 = $400,000. The $100,000 figure is the 20% of sales that comes from the other 1,600 customers.

questions.stem: An Edmonton car wash learns that a small group of heavy users who wash their cars weekly generates most of its revenue. Following the logic of usage-rate segmentation and the 80/20 rule, what should it do?
options: Create a frequency or loyalty program that rewards and retains the heavy users
Stop marketing to heavy users, since they will keep coming anyway
Shift all of its spending to non-users who live outside the city
Replace its usage data with census data on customers' ages and incomes
questions.explanation: Because a small share of heavy users produces most of the sales, protecting and rewarding them with frequency or loyalty programs is the classic 80/20 response. Ignoring them risks losing the customers who matter most.

questions.stem: A Montreal grocery chain sorts shoppers into heavy, medium, light and non-users of its in-store bakery, based on how many times they buy bakery items each month. This is segmentation by:
questions.explanation: Usage rate is the quantity consumed or patronage during a specific period, usually classified as heavy, medium, light and non-users. Benefits sought would group shoppers by what they want from the bakery, not by how often they buy.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts usage rate with loyalty status?
options: Usage rate measures a buyer's commitment to one brand; loyalty status measures the quantity consumed in a period
Usage rate is how much or how often a product is used in a period; loyalty status is commitment to one brand
Both measure the number of store visits in a period, so the two variables are interchangeable
Usage rate is a psychographic variable, while loyalty status is a demographic variable
questions.explanation: Usage rate = quantity or frequency in a period (heavy versus light users); loyalty status = commitment to a brand. A heavy user can still switch brands freely, and both variables are behaviouristic.

questions.stem: An industrial-cleaning supplier uses one sales approach for clients whose head office buys for every location, and a different approach for clients where each branch does its own buying. This business-market segmentation is based on:
questions.explanation: Centralized versus decentralized buying is a purchasing-approaches base. Operating characteristics describe the technology or capabilities a client has, not how it organizes its buying.

questions.stem: A Calgary pipe-fitting distributor creates a premium service for oil-field customers who need emergency parts delivered within hours, and it prices small rush orders differently from large planned orders. Which business segmentation base is this?
questions.explanation: Urgency, order size and specific application are situational factors. Purchasing approaches would focus on how the customer organizes its buying (centralized or decentralized, buying criteria), not on the urgency of a particular order.

questions.stem: In business markets, the technology a customer uses, whether it is a user or non-user of a product, and its capabilities all fall under which segmentation base?
questions.explanation: Technology, user status and capabilities are operating characteristics. Note that user status is behaviouristic in consumer markets but sits under operating characteristics in business markets.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the additional bases that businesses use to segment business markets?
questions.explanation: Lifestyle and personality are psychographic variables used to segment CONSUMER markets. The additional B2B bases are operating characteristics, purchasing approaches, situational factors and personal characteristics (which describe individual buyers' traits such as risk attitude, not their lifestyle).

questions.stem: A software vendor groups its corporate clients by NAICS industry code and number of employees, and separately by how risk-averse their individual buyers are. Which classification is correct?
options: Both groupings are operating characteristics, because both describe how the client company runs
NAICS code and employees are demographic bases; buyers' attitude toward risk is a personal-characteristics base
NAICS code is a situational factor; buyers' attitude toward risk is a purchasing approach
Both groupings are psychographic variables borrowed directly from consumer markets
questions.explanation: Industry code, number of employees, sales and location are business demographics. Attitude toward risk, buyer-seller similarity and loyalty are personal characteristics of the individuals who do the buying.

questions.stem: Character descriptions of a brand's typical customer are called:
questions.explanation: Personas are character descriptions of a brand's typical customer. A market segment is the group itself; the persona brings its typical member to life.

questions.stem: Bow River Bank's marketing team writes up 'Kayla, the Planner': 29, works in HR in Calgary, is saving for a condo, reads personal-finance blogs and values security. The write-up includes a photo and a personal quote. What has the team created?
questions.explanation: A named, story-like character description of the typical customer is a persona. A positioning statement describes the brand ('For ... who desire ..., [brand] is the ...'), not the customer.

questions.stem: How does a persona differ from a market segment?
options: A persona is a group of buyers with common needs, while a segment is a single fictional customer
A segment is a group of buyers with common needs; a persona is a character representing its typical customer
A persona plots competing brands on two perceptual dimensions, while a segment lists products
A persona states the brand's single competitive advantage, while a segment states its price
questions.explanation: The segment is the group; the persona is a single character representing its typical member. The reversed version is the trap, and plotting brands on two dimensions describes a perceptual map.

questions.stem: Why do marketers build personas for their target markets?
options: To replace the need to identify and size market segments at all
To display competing brands on a two-dimensional graph of consumer perceptions
To make the typical customer concrete so product, message and media decisions fit that person
To calculate how the firm's sales split between heavy users and light users
questions.explanation: Personas turn segment data into a relatable person, so teams design offerings and communications for that customer's needs and media habits. They build on segmentation instead of replacing it.

questions.stem: A detailed target market profile or persona would typically include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: demographic details such as age and occupation
psychographic details such as values and interests
a competitor's production costs per unit
media habits such as favourite apps and podcasts
questions.explanation: Profiles and personas describe the customer: demographics, psychographics, media habits and needs. A competitor's production costs describe the competitor, not the target customer.

questions.stem: A Toronto retailer wants to know which specific neighbourhood population clusters, with names like 'Middle-Class Mosaic', live near a proposed store site. Which source best fits this need?
options: A market-product grid of its own products
questions.explanation: Environics Analytics (PRIZM) provides granular data that pinpoints population clusters such as 'Middle-Class Mosaic'. Nielsen and Euromonitor provide broader, general consumer and lifestyle trends.

questions.stem: According to the course, how does data from Nielsen or Euromonitor differ from Environics Analytics' data?
options: Nielsen and Euromonitor provide granular neighbourhood clusters; Environics provides only global trends
All three companies provide only perceptual maps of competing brands
Nielsen and Euromonitor provide general consumer and lifestyle trends; Environics pinpoints population clusters
Environics provides positioning statements; Nielsen and Euromonitor provide personas
questions.explanation: General trends come from research companies like Nielsen and Euromonitor; Environics Analytics works at a more granular level, identifying population clusters. The reversed version is the trap.

questions.stem: Companies such as Environics Analytics provide data on a more _____ basis, pinpointing information on population clusters.
questions.explanation: Environics data is granular: fine-grained enough to pinpoint population clusters. 'General' describes the consumer and lifestyle trend data from Nielsen or Euromonitor.

questions.stem: A national beverage brand wants a broad picture of how Canadian consumer and lifestyle trends are shifting before it plans the next three years. Which source does the course suggest for this kind of overview?
options: A PRIZM cluster profile for one postal code
A persona written by its own sales team
A research company such as Nielsen or Euromonitor
questions.explanation: For general consumer and lifestyle trends, the course points to research companies such as Nielsen or Euromonitor. A single PRIZM cluster is granular and local: useful for pinpointing neighbourhoods, not for a national trend overview.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of segmentation analytics as described in the course?
questions.explanation: A positioning statement is a formal description of a brand's image and what sets it apart; it isn't segmentation data. Nielsen, Euromonitor and Environics Analytics are the data sources the course names.

questions.stem: What is the FIRST step in the six-step process for segmenting a market?
options: Cluster common consumer variables to create meaningful segments
Identify consumer/customer needs and common characteristics in the market
Estimate the size and feasibility of each segment
Identify the segment(s) to be targeted
questions.explanation: The process starts by identifying customer needs and common characteristics. Clustering (step 2) can't happen until the firm knows which needs and characteristics to group buyers on.

questions.stem: In the six-step segmentation process, which step comes immediately AFTER 'cluster common consumer/customer variables to create meaningful market segments'?
options: Estimate the size and feasibility of each segment
Identify the segment(s) to be targeted
Take actions with marketing programs to reach the segment(s)
Identify consumer needs and common characteristics
questions.explanation: Step 2 (cluster) is followed by step 3: estimate the size and feasibility of each segment. Choosing targets is step 4, because firms must size segments before deciding which to pursue.

questions.stem: What is the FIFTH step in the six-step process for segmenting a market?
options: Monitor and evaluate the success of these programs compared with objectives
Take actions with marketing programs to reach the segment(s)
Identify the segment(s) to be targeted
Estimate the size and feasibility of each segment
questions.explanation: Step 5 is taking action with marketing programs to reach the chosen segment(s). Monitoring and evaluating against objectives is step 6, the final step.

questions.stem: Sunridge Cycles launched ads and new store displays aimed at its 'family weekend rider' segment. Six months later, it compares family-bike sales against the targets it set at the start. Which step of the segmentation process is it in?
options: Step 6: monitor and evaluate the success of these programs compared with objectives
Step 5: take actions with marketing programs to reach the segment(s)
Step 3: estimate the size and feasibility of each segment
Step 4: identify the segment(s) to be targeted
questions.explanation: Comparing results with objectives is step 6. The campaign launch was step 5; this is the evaluation that follows it.

questions.stem: A Kelowna winery has interviewed buyers about what they look for in wine. It now groups people who share similar characteristics into meaningful categories such as 'gift buyers', 'weekend entertainers' and 'serious collectors'. It has not yet estimated how big each group is. Which step is the winery in?
options: Step 2: cluster common variables to create meaningful market segments
Step 1: identify needs and common characteristics
Step 3: estimate the size and feasibility of each segment
Step 4: identify the segment(s) to be targeted
questions.explanation: Grouping buyers who share variables into meaningful segments is step 2 (cluster). The interviews about needs were step 1, and estimating each group's size comes next, in step 3.

questions.stem: Using census data and sales records, the Kelowna winery estimates that its 'serious collectors' and 'gift buyers' segments are both large and realistic to serve, while 'weekend entertainers' is small. It now decides to pursue collectors and gift buyers. Which step is this decision?
options: Step 4: identify the segment(s) to be targeted
Step 5: take actions with marketing programs
questions.explanation: Choosing which segments to pursue is step 4. The sizing work just completed was step 3, and designing campaigns to reach the chosen segments will be step 5.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the six steps in the process for segmenting a market?
options: Estimate the size and feasibility of each segment
Write a positioning statement for each competitor
Monitor and evaluate the success of these programs compared with objectives
Cluster common consumer variables to create meaningful market segments
questions.explanation: Positioning statements are written for one's own brand during positioning; they aren't a step in segmenting. The six steps are: identify needs, cluster, estimate size and feasibility, identify targets, take action, and monitor/evaluate.

questions.stem: Why does 'estimate the size and feasibility of each segment' come BEFORE 'identify the segment(s) to be targeted'?
options: Because targeting must be finished before any segments can be formed or clustered
Because a firm can't sensibly choose targets until it knows how large and reachable each segment is
Because the marketing program for each segment is launched during the estimating step
Because feasibility can only be judged after results are monitored against objectives
questions.explanation: Size and feasibility are the evidence for choosing targets; without them, the choice is guesswork. The marketing program is launched in step 5 and monitoring happens in step 6, both after targeting.

questions.stem: A framework that relates the market segments of potential buyers to the products offered or potential marketing actions is a:
questions.explanation: That is a market-product grid: segments on one side (rows), products or marketing actions on the other (columns), and estimated market size in the cells. A perceptual map plots brands by consumer perceptions instead.

questions.stem: Polar Bikes builds a table with buyer segments (commuters, mountain riders, kids) as rows and its bike models as columns. It writes the estimated market size in each cell to see where to focus. What tool is this?
questions.explanation: Segments in rows, products in columns and estimated market size in each cell make a market-product grid. A perceptual map would plot brands on two consumer-perception dimensions.

questions.stem: How does a market-product grid differ from a perceptual map?
options: A grid plots brands on two perceptual dimensions, while a perceptual map lists segments against products
A grid relates segments to products with estimated market sizes; a perceptual map plots how consumers see brands
Both show consumers' perceptions of brands; they differ only in how the chart is formatted
A grid is used only for positioning, while a perceptual map is used only for segmentation
questions.explanation: The grid is a segmentation/targeting tool that shows where market volume lies across segment-product combinations. The perceptual map is a positioning tool that shows where brands sit in consumers' minds. The swapped version is the trap.

questions.stem: On Polar Bikes' market-product grid, the 'kids' row shows a large estimated market in the 'balance bike' column but a tiny one in the 'carbon road bike' column. What does this suggest Polar should do?
options: Reposition its carbon road bikes as premium children's toys
Drop the kids' segment entirely and focus on adult riders
Focus its kids' marketing on balance bikes, not carbon road bikes
Cut carbon road bike prices for kids until that cell grows
questions.explanation: The cells show estimated market size, so the large kids/balance-bike cell is where the opportunity lies. Dropping the whole segment would ignore that strong cell, and nothing in the grid calls for repositioning carbon bikes.

questions.stem: Which statement about a market-product grid is NOT correct?
options: Columns typically represent products or marketing actions
It plots brands by how consumers perceive them on two attributes
Cells typically show the estimated size of the market
questions.explanation: Plotting brands by consumer perception on two attributes describes a perceptual map. The grid relates segments (rows) to products or marketing actions (columns), with estimated market sizes in the cells.

questions.stem: A payday-loan company runs flashy ads concentrated in low-income neighbourhoods, aimed at people who are already struggling with debt. Critics call the campaign exploitative. Which ethical segmentation concern does this most directly raise?
options: Targeting a segment with poor expected growth
Relying on an inaccurate perceptual map
questions.explanation: Aiming high-cost loans at people in financial hardship is targeting a disadvantaged group, one of the legal and ethical issues the course lists. Expected growth is a selecting criterion, not an ethical concern.

questions.stem: The course lists several legal and ethical issues marketers must consider when segmenting and targeting. Which is NOT one of them?
options: Using the 80/20 rule to reward heavy users
questions.explanation: The listed issues are consumer backlash, vulnerable groups, disadvantaged groups and potentially harmful products. Rewarding heavy users through loyalty programs is a standard usage-rate tactic, not one of the listed ethical issues.

questions.stem: According to the course, when can social responsibility be more important than profits in segmentation and targeting?
options: Only when a segment fails to meet the firm's ROI target
Only in not-for-profit and government organizations
Whenever a firm uses mass marketing instead of segmenting
When the marketing is viewed as exploitative or irresponsible
questions.explanation: The slides state that social responsibility can be more important than profits if marketing is viewed as exploitative or irresponsible. This applies to all firms, not just not-for-profits, and isn't tied to ROI targets.

questions.stem: A Canadian energy-drink brand discovers that its fastest-growing segment is 13- to 15-year-olds. Based on the course's guidance on socially responsible segmentation, what should it do?
options: Avoid targeting this vulnerable group with a potentially harmful product
Target the group aggressively, because its expected growth is so high
Reposition the drink as a breakfast product for children and teens
Run head-to-head ads against rival energy drinks aimed at young teens
questions.explanation: Young teens are a vulnerable group and energy drinks are potentially harmful, so targeting them risks harm and consumer backlash. High expected growth is a selecting criterion, but the course says social responsibility can outweigh profit.

questions.stem: Because segmentation is legal, marketers never need to worry about consumer backlash when they choose which groups to target.
questions.explanation: False. Corrected statement: marketers must avoid consumer backlash, especially when targeting vulnerable or disadvantaged groups or marketing potentially harmful products, and social responsibility can matter more than profits.

questions.stem: The impression of a branded product that a marketer wants to establish in consumers' minds, relative to their needs and in contrast to the competition, is called:
questions.explanation: That is product positioning: the place the product occupies in consumers' minds relative to competitors. Product differentiation is using features and advertising to make products seem different and better.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the three basic factors on which product positioning is built?
questions.explanation: The three basic positioning factors are image, product attributes and price. Market size is a criterion for selecting target segments.

questions.stem: Summit Skincare positions its new serum as a premium, dermatologist-grade luxury product. Which marketing decision would most UNDERMINE that position?
options: Featuring clinical test results in its ads
Using heavy glass packaging with a minimalist design
Selling it in discount bins at dollar stores
questions.explanation: For positioning to succeed, all marketing mix efforts must support it. Discount-bin distribution contradicts a premium image, while the other choices reinforce it.

questions.stem: Once a brand has established its position, how does the course say that position should be maintained?
options: By changing the advertising message every month to stay fresh
By matching every competitor's price cut immediately
By targeting every segment in the market
questions.explanation: Positions are maintained through consistent performance and communication. Constantly changing the message or chasing every segment blurs the place the brand holds in consumers' minds.

questions.stem: Chiquita put its brand sticker on bananas, a fruit most shoppers saw as an unbranded commodity, and promoted them as consistently high-quality. This created a distinct place for the brand in consumers' minds where none had existed before. This best illustrates:
questions.explanation: Creating a brand's first distinct place in consumers' minds is product positioning. Repositioning changes a place a product already occupies, but Chiquita was establishing a position for a previously unbranded commodity.

questions.stem: Children's Advil pain reliever positioned itself against Children's Tylenol pain reliever by running ads, which claimed that the Advil brand is superior because it works faster and longer than the Tylenol brand. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Head-to-head positioning means competing directly with competitors on similar product attributes in the same target market; here, speed and duration of relief for the same parents. 'Lateral', 'consumer' and 'cognitive' positioning are not course terms.

questions.stem: There are a lot of skateboard manufacturers on the market, but the BMW Streetcarver is the only one with stabilizers and wheel design based on BMW's automobile. This technology gives the BMW Streetcarver better control at high speeds and around sharp turns than any other brand. What type of positioning is BMW using with its skateboard priced at $495?
questions.explanation: Differentiation positioning means seeking a smaller, less-competitive niche by stressing unique attributes: the only board with BMW-based stabilizers, at a premium price. It isn't head-to-head, because BMW isn't fighting mainstream boards on the same attributes for the same buyers.

questions.stem: Competing directly with competitors on similar product attributes in the same target market is called:
questions.explanation: That is head-to-head positioning. Differentiation positioning does the opposite: it avoids direct competition by seeking a smaller, less-competitive niche.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts head-to-head positioning with differentiation positioning?
options: Head-to-head competes on similar attributes in the same market; differentiation positioning seeks a smaller, less-competitive niche
Head-to-head seeks a smaller, less-competitive niche; differentiation positioning attacks the market leader directly
Head-to-head changes an existing position; differentiation positioning creates a brand's very first position
Both terms mean selling several different products to several different market segments
questions.explanation: Head-to-head = same market, similar attributes, direct comparison. Differentiation positioning = a niche, unique attributes, less competition. Changing an existing position is repositioning, and selling different products to different segments is product differentiation.

questions.stem: Kestrel Audio stays out of the crowded wireless-earbud market dominated by large brands. Instead, it makes the only earbuds designed for competitive swimmers, waterproof to 10 metres with bone-conduction sound, and sells them to that small group at a premium price. This is:
questions.explanation: Seeking a smaller, less-competitive niche and stressing unique attributes is differentiation positioning. It isn't head-to-head, because Kestrel deliberately avoids competing with the big brands on similar attributes in the mainstream market.

questions.stem: Why might a small firm with a genuinely unique product feature choose differentiation positioning instead of head-to-head positioning?
options: It requires the firm to match the market leader's attributes exactly and then win on price in the same market
Head-to-head positioning is permitted only for products that have already reached the decline stage
It guarantees the firm the largest possible share of the total market within its first year
It avoids direct battles with larger rivals by placing the brand in a smaller, less-competitive niche that values its unique attributes
questions.explanation: Differentiation positioning means seeking a less-competitive, smaller niche by stressing unique attributes, which suits a small firm that can't win a direct fight. Matching the leader's attributes in the same market describes head-to-head positioning.

questions.stem: A formalized statement that identifies the image a branded product represents in the market and what sets it apart from the competition is a:
questions.explanation: That is a positioning statement. A USP is the single competitive advantage a brand may build its positioning on; the positioning statement is the full sentence naming target, need, brand, category and benefits.

questions.stem: Complete the course's positioning statement template: 'For (target market) who desire (target market need), (brand) is the _____ that offers (product benefits).'
questions.explanation: The template is: For (target market) who desire (target market need), (brand) is the (product category) that offers (product benefits). Competitors, price points and channels are not slots in the template.

questions.stem: Which of the following follows the course's positioning statement format?
options: For busy parents who desire quick dinners, FreshFork is the meal kit that offers pre-chopped ingredients
FreshFork: quick, healthy dinners made easy for busy Calgary families every night!
FreshFork aims to increase its market share in Calgary by 10 percent by the end of next year
FreshFork earns 80 percent of its sales from the 20 percent of customers who order weekly
questions.explanation: Only the 'For busy parents who desire quick dinners...' sentence fills every slot of the template: target market, need ('who desire'), brand, product category and benefits. The others are a slogan, a sales objective and an 80/20 observation.

questions.stem: Arbor Tea's draft positioning statement reads: 'For health-conscious professionals, Arbor is the tea brand that offers organic, antioxidant-rich blends.' Which element of the course template is missing?
questions.explanation: The draft names the target (health-conscious professionals), the brand (Arbor), the category (tea brand) and the benefits (organic, antioxidant-rich blends), but it skips the 'who desire (need)' clause.

questions.stem: How does a positioning statement differ from a unique selling proposition (USP)?
options: A positioning statement names the target, need, brand, category and benefits; a USP is the one advantage it may rest on
A USP names the target, need, category and benefits, while a positioning statement is one single advantage
A positioning statement plots brands on two axes, while a USP lists market segments against products
A USP is used only during segmentation, while a positioning statement is used only during targeting
questions.explanation: The positioning statement is the full template sentence; the USP is one distinctive advantage that may appear inside it as the product benefit. The reversed version is the trap.

questions.stem: A perceptual map shows how various drinks are seen in the minds of adult consumers. On its vertical axis (more nutritious at the top, less nutritious at the bottom), coffee sits above sugared soft drinks, while skinny lattes and fruit-flavoured drinks sit above coffee. Suppose a coffee producer wants to increase sales. Its advertising agency recommends that it run ads showing that coffee is healthier than one or more competitive drinks shown on the map. In the ads, coffee should be compared with:
options: fruit-flavoured drinks and sugared soft drinks.
both sugared soft drinks and skinny lattes.
questions.explanation: The coffee producer should compare itself only with drinks that are lower than coffee on the vertical nutrition axis, which consumers see as less nutritious. The only such drink is sugared soft drinks; skinny lattes and fruit-flavoured drinks are perceived as more nutritious than coffee, so claiming to beat them would not be believed.

questions.stem: A means of displaying or graphing, in two dimensions, the location of products or brands in the minds of consumers is a:
questions.explanation: That is a perceptual map. A market-product grid relates segments to products with estimated market sizes; it doesn't show consumer perceptions.

questions.stem: Huron Hotels surveys travellers about six hotel brands and plots each brand on a chart with 'price' on one axis and 'perceived luxury' on the other. It then spots an empty area for an affordable-but-luxurious hotel. What tool did Huron use?
questions.explanation: Plotting brands on two dimensions based on consumer perceptions is a perceptual map, and spotting empty spaces is one of its main uses. A market-product grid shows segments and products, not perceived brand positions.

questions.stem: What is a primary reason marketers use perceptual maps?
options: To calculate the market size of each segment-product combination
To see how consumers perceive competing brands and to find positioning gaps
To assign each customer to a segment at the lowest possible cost
To estimate how the firm's sales split between heavy and light users
questions.explanation: Perceptual maps show where brands sit in consumers' minds relative to rivals, revealing close competitors, open gaps and possible moves. Estimating market size for each segment-product cell is the job of a market-product grid.

questions.stem: Students often confuse perceptual maps with repositioning. Which statement is accurate?
options: Repositioning is the display tool, while the perceptual map is the strategy that changes a brand's image
A perceptual map shows sales by segment, while repositioning shows changes in a product's price
A perceptual map shows where brands sit in consumers' minds; repositioning is the strategy of changing that place
Both are steps within the six-step process for segmenting a market
questions.explanation: The perceptual map is a display tool; repositioning is a strategy that changes the place a product occupies in consumers' minds, which can show up as a move on the map. That is why 'perceptual mapping' is the wrong answer in the Grape-Nuts question.

questions.stem: Post Grape-Nuts cereal has been marketed since early in the 20th century. Its market share has been steadily declining as consumers began associating it with something their grandfather ate. Post recently launched a campaign which invited consumers to try the crunchy cereal on top of their yogurt, their salad, or their bowl of soup as a delicious addition. This is an example of a _____ strategy.
questions.explanation: Repositioning changes the place an existing product occupies in consumers' minds; here, from an old-fashioned breakfast cereal to an all-day topping. 'Product positioning' is tempting, but the brand already had a position and Post is changing it.

questions.stem: Changing the place a product occupies in consumers' minds relative to competitive products, to more accurately meet consumer needs, is called:
questions.explanation: That is repositioning. Product positioning establishes a product's place in the first place; repositioning changes a place that already exists.

questions.stem: What separates repositioning from product positioning?
options: Repositioning is done before launch, while positioning is done only after sales decline
Repositioning applies only to services, while positioning applies only to goods
Positioning changes a product's price, while repositioning changes only its packaging
Positioning establishes a brand's place in consumers' minds; repositioning changes a place it already holds
questions.explanation: Repositioning assumes an existing position that no longer fits consumer needs. The timing in the 'before launch' option is reversed: a brand-new product gets positioned, and an established one gets repositioned.

questions.stem: Ridgeline Games was long seen as a maker of dusty family board games that only grandparents bought. It launched strategy-heavy games, streamer partnerships and sleek packaging, and young adults now see it as a cool brand for game nights. This is:
questions.explanation: Changing an established, dated image so the brand occupies a new place in consumers' minds is repositioning. It isn't head-to-head positioning, because the stem describes no direct comparison with a rival on similar attributes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of repositioning?
options: A baking-soda brand promotes its product as a fridge deodorizer to expand use beyond baking
A dated department store refreshes its image to attract younger shoppers
A start-up launches its first-ever product and creates its initial brand image
A breakfast cereal is promoted as an all-day snack
questions.explanation: A brand-new product's first image is positioning, not repositioning, because there is no existing place to change. The other examples change how an existing product is seen or used.

questions.stem: Every major grocery chain in Canada, including Harvest Basket, offers fresh produce, an in-store bakery, free parking and a loyalty card. For Harvest Basket, these features are best described as:
questions.explanation: Associations shared with other brands are points-of-parity: the basics needed to compete in the category, as in the course's Sobeys example. They can't be points-of-difference, because shoppers can find them to the same extent at rival chains.

questions.stem: Attributes or benefits that consumers strongly associate with a brand, positively evaluate, and believe they could not find to the same extent with a competitive brand are:
questions.explanation: That is the definition of points-of-difference (PODs). Points-of-parity are associations that may be shared with other brands.

questions.stem: Coffee drinkers strongly associate Northern Grind with its signature maple-cinnamon latte and its community hockey sponsorships, rate both very positively, and say no other chain offers anything quite like them. These associations are best described as:
questions.explanation: Strong association, positive evaluation and a belief that rivals can't match it are the three marks of a point-of-difference, as in the course's Tim Hortons example. Points-of-parity are shared with competitors.

questions.stem: Customers of Glacier Cafe really like its free Wi-Fi, but every nearby competitor offers equally fast free Wi-Fi. Why is the Wi-Fi a point-of-parity rather than a point-of-difference for Glacier?
options: Because customers evaluate the free Wi-Fi negatively overall
Because although valued, it is available to the same extent at competing brands
Because Wi-Fi is a price factor rather than a product attribute
Because points-of-difference must always relate to the brand's price
questions.explanation: A POD must be strongly associated with the brand, positively evaluated AND not available to the same extent from rivals. The Wi-Fi is liked, but it fails the uniqueness test, so it is a POP.

questions.stem: Why does a brand need both points-of-parity and points-of-difference?
options: POPs show it meets the category basics (ticket to play); PODs give a reason to choose it over rivals (reason to win)
POPs make the brand unique, while PODs show it is similar to brands consumers already know
POPs are needed only by service brands, while PODs are needed only by brands of physical goods
Only PODs matter for positioning; POPs are features consumers simply ignore when choosing
questions.explanation: Without POPs, consumers may not see the brand as a real option in the category; without PODs, they have no reason to prefer it. The reversed version (POPs = unique) is the trap.

questions.stem: When a firm bases its positioning on one single, distinctive competitive advantage, that advantage is called its:
questions.explanation: Choosing one competitive advantage as the basis for positioning means building on a unique selling proposition; the alternative is positioning on multiple differences. A point-of-parity is shared with rivals, so it can't serve as a USP.

questions.stem: Swift Pizza repeats one message on every ad, menu and box: 'Hot at your door in 20 minutes or it's free.' It does not promote taste, price or variety. Swift is basing its positioning on:
questions.explanation: Building positioning around one distinctive benefit and communicating it consistently is a USP strategy. A multiple-differences strategy would promote several advantages at once.

questions.stem: When choosing a competitive advantage on which to base positioning, how does a USP approach differ from a multiple-differences approach?
options: A USP approach promotes several shared benefits, while a multiple-differences approach promotes just one
A USP is always based on price, while multiple differences are always based on image
A USP is used for segmentation, while multiple differences are used for targeting
A USP approach promotes one distinctive advantage; a multiple-differences approach promotes several ways the brand differs
questions.explanation: The course frames the choice as one unique selling proposition versus multiple differences. Both are positioning decisions, and neither is limited to price or image.

questions.stem: Slumber North Mattress's research shows that the one advantage consumers truly value, and that rivals cannot match, is a patented cooling layer. If it wants a single, clear basis for its positioning, what should it do?
options: Make the cooling layer its USP and communicate it consistently
Promote that it offers the same features as every competitor
Reposition as a discount brand and compete mainly on price
Abandon positioning and switch to an undifferentiated mass-market approach
questions.explanation: A valued advantage that rivals can't match is ideal as a USP, and positions are maintained through consistent communication. Promoting shared features only stresses points-of-parity, which give no reason to choose the brand.

questions.stem: Which of the following would NOT make a good unique selling proposition?
options: A distinctive benefit that customers value highly
An advantage that competitors cannot easily match
A benefit that every competitor offers equally well
A single, clear reason to choose the brand
questions.explanation: A benefit every competitor offers equally well is a point-of-parity; it gives no reason to choose one brand over another. A good USP is distinctive, valued and hard to copy.
